When you say sigma approx 0.6 / sqrt(D), is density the # bears per 100km2? I calculated sigma as half the home range radius, but maybe I misunderstood how to calculate that.

As for misunderstanding regarding the intercept of the detection function, that is what I meant when I referred to it as the "probability of detection," sorry for the confusion!

The current bear density estimate I've been using as a pilot value is probably closer to the density of bears within our pilot region, but I agree, it will vary across the state. Do you suggest I fit potential trap configurations to different bear densities and choose a configuration that will maximize precision given a level of effort across the different potential densities?

Once a trapping configuration is selected, is there a way to export the trap locations as shapefiles?

Thanks again!

Laura

The principles of stratification transfer from other spatial sampling, but care is needed in the SECR modelling when effort is stratified.

> For systematic designs I don't think bias is an issue for SECR as long as you avoid designs with pathological spacing (cluster << home range size, within-cluster spacing > home range diameter) (of course if your spatial sampling is not representative you will get the wrong answer). >
> I'm sceptical of your pilot values. I do not believe there are 0.37 black bears per sq km across half of Wisconsin. sigma = 1 km is small, and overall detection probability scales with sigma^2, so this is a sensitive issue. messages.subject: Re: Study design over large region
messages.body_plain:
Halfnormal sigma approx 0.6 / sqrt(D) works for D and sigma in consistent units - most simply km and km^2 in your case (if you specify D in bears/100km^2 then sigma is in units of 10 km). That relies on a crude global relationship between home-range size and density as in Ecography 39:676-688. Usually halfnormal sigma is somewhat less than half the 95% HR radius (r approx 2.45 sigma).

"Do you suggest I fit potential trap configurations to different bear densities and choose a configuration that will maximize precision given a level of effort across the different potential densities?"

Broadly speaking, yes, but I'm loath to commit because (i) ideally for a study of this size (and cost) one would think about stratification, and (ii) it seems unlikely that all you want is a single number for the state - this is a chance to quantify uneven spatial distribution as well. Perhaps your pilot needs to try both low and high density areas?

"Once a trapping configuration is selected, is there a way to export the trap locations as shapefiles?"

Not in a single function. It is a 2-step operation; for example (i) form a SpatialPointsDataFrame object (package sp) (ii) export that using writeOGR (package rgdal). Note
i. A SPDF requires a dataframe of attribute information; if your traps object does not have covariates, you'll have to make one up.
ii. First coerce the traps object (a dataframe) to a matrix
iii. You will want your shapefile to have projection information, so specify that when making your SPDF. Finding the right specification is the hard bit. See ?writeGPS for a Maryland UTM example.

Change c:/temp to the folder you want to use.
.
library(secr)
xy <- as.matrix(traps(possumCH))
someattributes <- data.frame(num = 1:nrow(xy))
spdf <- sp::SpatialPointsDataFrame(xy, someattributes, proj4string = CRS("+proj=nzmg"))
rgdal::writeOGR(spdf, layer = 'possumtraps', 'C:/temp', driver="ESRI Shapefile")

messages.body_plain:

When one models differences between groups of animals (say sexes) using an individual covariate and the conditional likelihood, it is easy to obtain either group-specific or total densities, with associated measures of uncertainty using derived().

Is there also an easy way to get total densities with associated measures of uncertainty if one models these differences as groups using the full likelihood (e.g. using predict())?

Thanks,
Eric

messages.subject: Re: total density across groups
messages.body_plain:
Hello there
An interesting challenge while I chew on my breakfast muesli! I think you can do it by specifying the contrasts used to code levels of the group factor.

>From a vignette coming soon to a CRAN mirror near you...

Footnote 10 says 'this also works in secr'. Try running the following code. Note x 2 (number of groups) scales mean to total.
Murray

library(secr)

## generate some fake groups and fit model
covariates(captdata) <- data.frame(sex = sample(c('F','M'), nrow(captdata), p = c(0.4,0.6), replace = TRUE))
fitg <- secr.fit(captdata, model = D~g, groups = 'sex')
## refit model with contrasts
fitgt <- secr.fit(captdata, model=D~g, groups = 'sex', details = list(contrasts=list(g = contr.sum)))

## checking results...
## same likelihood
AIC(fitg, fitgt)
## different coefficients
coef(fitg)
coef(fitgt)
## same group-specific estimates
predict(fitg)
predict(fitgt)

## now compare estimates of total density
## sum of group-specific densities
sum(sapply(predict(fitg), '[[', 'D', 'estimate'))
## backtransformed from recoded
exp(coef(fitgt)['D','beta']) * 2

## using identity link to dodge back-transformation bias
fitgi <- secr.fit(captdata, model = D~g, groups = 'sex', link = list(D='identity'))
fitgti <- secr.fit(captdata, model=D~g, groups = 'sex', details = list(contrasts=list(g = contr.sum)), link = list(D='identity'))
## sum of group-specific densities
sum(sapply(predict(fitgi), '[[', 'D', 'estimate'))
## backtransformed from recoded
coef(fitgti)['D',c('beta', 'lcl','ucl')]*2

messages.subject: openCR 1.1.1
messages.body_plain:
openCR is a new R package for open-population analyses of spatial or non-spatial capture-recapture data. You can get it from CRAN however you usually install R packages (OS X binaries will be available in a day or two). See https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/openCR.html for features, examples and limitations. The models extend Schwarz and Arnason (1996) and Borchers and Efford (2008). The parameterization of recruitment is flexible (options include population growth rate and per capita recruitment). Cormack-Jolly-Seber and Pradel models are included. Spatially explicit analyses may assume home-range centres are fixed or allow dispersal between sampling sessions (experimental in 1.1.1). Fitting of non-spatial models is somewhat slower than in MARK and the non-spatial capability of openCR is limited. The next release (1.2) will use multithreaded C++ code, for a considerable improvement in speed.

Murray

messages.subject: Non-euclidean distance for multi-sessions
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm having trouble getting nedist to work for my multi-session data. I used the same script for my single session data earlier and it appeared to work. I'm using the script found in the secr-noneuclidean pdf.

I have four sessions, which are all neighbouring ranges, each range was sampled a different year. There is a large, wide river running through the study area as well as another large river on the northern edge. We know that these rivers act as complete barriers to movement for our species (a large ungulate). The script I'm using is below:

noneuc_mask2km <- make.mask (traps(CH), buffer = 60000, type = 'trapbuffer', spacing = 2000,
                           poly = rivers, poly.habitat = F)
noneuc_mask500m <- make.mask (traps(CH), buffer = 60000, type = 'trapbuffer', spacing = 500,
                             poly = rivers, poly.habitat = F)

userd <- nedist(traps(CH), noneuc_mask2km, noneuc_mask500m)
Error in rep(1, nrow(mask)) : invalid 'times' argument

I'm using two masks as recommended by Efford, with the alternative mask (500m) to base the calculations as the study area is very large (a few hundred kilometres) with lots of recaptures. I've done checks on my data when I brought it in and all appears to be okay. The poly = rivers is the rivers that are non-habitat.

Thanks for any help.

messages.body_plain:
I've never seen an error like that. You seem to be making a big analysis out of a small dataset (100 detections). Why 25k pixels? First I suggest reducing your detection (trap? time? animal?) covariates to 2-3 levels, and trying just one covariate at a time. 'secr' doesn't cope well with trap covariates, nor with any detection covariate that has many distinct values. Possibly you have measured something on a continuous scale at each of the 600 camera locations? If that works at all it will be very very slow to fit, for no real gain in insight.
Murray
